title: The perfect active and the principal parts

objectives.can: Recognise a perfect indicative active, parse it and connect it with its present.
Recognise ten more common verbs with their perfects.

explanation.summary: The perfect is the tense of narrative, and of the completed action: 'he said', 'they came and saw', 'what I have written'. Its endings differ from the other tenses, and its stem is not predictable from the present, so each verb has to be learned with four principal parts.

sections.heading: One tense, two English meanings
body: The Latin perfect names an action as a completed whole. It covers two English tenses: the simple past ('he said') and the present perfect ('he has said'). In John 19:22, *Quod scripsi, scripsi* is 'what I have written, I have written': Pilate speaks about something already done whose result stands. In John 1:39, *venerunt et viderunt* is a plain narrative: 'they came and they saw'.

Do not translate the Latin perfect mechanically as either. In a story it will usually be 'did'; in speech, when the result still matters, it will often be 'has done'. The imperfect is a different thing: in the same verse *manserunt* (perfect) tells that they stayed, while *erat* (imperfect) sets the scene, 'it was about the tenth hour'.

sections.heading: The perfect endings
body: The perfect has its own set of endings, the same for all verbs, added to the perfect stem: -i, -isti, -it, -imus, -istis, -erunt. There is an alternative third person plural in -ere (*habuere*, *fuere*), which you will see now and then. Unlike the present, these endings carry no connecting vowel that depends on the conjugation: *vocavit*, *habuit*, *dixit* all end in -it.

Two tips for the third person. The -it of the perfect looks like the -it of the third-conjugation present (*dicit*, *dixit*), but in the perfect it is attached to the perfect stem, which differs from the present stem. And in some verbs the present and the perfect are spelled alike (*venit*, 'he comes' or 'he came'): only the context shows which.

sections.heading: Four principal parts
body: The perfect stem is found from the third principal part: drop the final -i. The four parts are the first person singular of the present, the present infinitive, the first person singular of the perfect, and a fourth part, usually the neuter of the perfect passive participle (the 'supine' form in -um). A dictionary entry such as *dico*, *dicere*, *dixi*, *dictum* gives you all four. From the first you build the present system (present, imperfect, future); from the third the whole perfect system; from the fourth the participle and the perfect passive.
The table of principal parts gives eight verbs. The first and third parts are forms in the texts; the infinitives and fourth parts are shown with a hyphen to mark the part that follows the stem.

sections.heading: Four ways of making the perfect stem
body: A large group of verbs, especially in the first and fourth conjugations, add -v- (*vocavi*, *audivi*); many in the second add -u- (*habui*, *timui*). Many in the third add -s- (*dixi*, *scripsi*, *misi*, *duxi*), and the s may combine with the last consonant of the stem. A few verbs lengthen the stem vowel, with or without a change of quality (*vidi*, *feci*, and with a change of vowel *egi*). A few reduplicate: the first consonant and a vowel are repeated before the stem (*steti*, *didici*).

These are patterns, not rules. Many verbs have a perfect that fits none of them neatly, and you learn the perfect with the verb. The editions sometimes print -u- for -v- (*audiui*, *amaui* for *audivi*), so look past the spelling of v and u.

misunderstandings: The perfect is not 'the past tense of the present stem': *dixit* is not formed from *dicit* by any rule, and the perfect of a verb cannot always be guessed. Learn the third principal part.
-erunt is the third person plural of the perfect; the -unt of the present (*dicunt*) is a different ending. *dixerunt* is 'they said' and *dicunt* 'they say'.
The perfect is not always English 'has': in narrative *vidit* is 'he saw'. The Latin does not tell you which; the context does.
Do not confuse the perfect with the imperfect. *videbat* is 'he was seeing, used to see'; *vidit* is 'he saw (on one occasion)'.

deeper.heading: Two Latin tenses in one
body: Historically the Latin perfect combines two older tenses: a perfect proper (the present result of a past action) and an aorist (a simple past event). Greek keeps these apart, and Latin joined them, which is why the single Latin form has two English equivalents. This is the usual account in the historical grammars.

examples.analysis: Four perfects in the two halves of one saying. *vidisti* and *credidisti* are second person singular, with -isti: 'you have seen', 'you have believed'. *viderunt* and *crediderunt* are third person plural, with -erunt: 'they have seen', 'they have believed'. The perfect stems vid- and credid- are not the present stems vide- and cred-: the perfect has to be learned with the verb. The perfect here states a result that stands.
